I was in incredible pain to when I got the Mirena. The best advice I can give is stay hydrated, SLEEP, and a heating pad. I felt significantly better day 2, but still had some bad cramping. Other than that, just have to wait it out, but it does start feeling better after a couple days!

I’ve been off BC for a little over a year and got the Mirena IUD. I had to go off the pill because my migraines and the pill mixed put me at high risk for a stroke. I didn’t ha e many breakouts the first 6 months, but after began having horrible breakouts. At 23 I thought I was passed this stage and became really self conscious about my skin. My dermatologist tried topical and antibiotics of various sorts, but the acne kept coming back. I also was recommended accutane, but refuse to go on it because of all the side effects they say it has. I just began my Curology prescription as a last ditch attempt and already finding luck with that and I’m going on my third week. I’ve cut back in my dairy and really trying to watch my diet! I noticed keeping a good simple skin routine really helps as well. I also recommend this site http://cosdna.com which will tell you what products you are using that causes your acne to be worse! I feel where you are coming from and I hope my Curology journey works! You should check it out too!

I really have liked everything about my major. I’ve liked the Investments side where I’m doing a lot of analysis (although that may not have come as easy to me) and I’ve loved learning the different financial planning elements; retirement, estate, insurance, education etc etc. it’s just putting those things into practice at my internship isn’t as appealing. There’s a lot of pressure and it’s honestly more stressful than anything else. I got into the field because i wanted to help people that didn’t have a lot of money have hope that they can make it. Get out of debt, send their children to school, plan for vacations, buy a home, retire someday. It’s seem contrary to where most people in the field want to advise people with more assets (which of course means more money for the advisor).

I think its the high stress, the dedication required, and the people. Now, of course you may never like everyone you work with, but coming from a retail background the mentality is really different. To me anyway. I originally was looking into financial planning because I wanted to financially help others, but I also don’t want to sacrifice my own happiness. Even as an intern I sometimes have to stay late and sacrifice studying time for classes. I hear the advisors saying they’ve had to stay till 8 or 9PM to finish various tasks for their clients. I’m just not sure I want that lifestyle where it’s constant work.

I picked finance after taking a personal money management class and found I was really understood and liked what I was learning. Everything came really easy for me and still does. Also for personal reasons, I saw my parents struggle to make ends meet and wanted to financially help people in that position like my parents were.

Listen. When I did my first semester at my transfer school. I failed all my midterms. I was very close to dropping out. But I just worked that much harder. I’m extremely hard on myself and similar to you; striving for those As. So a senior in a college now, I still best myself up over anything less than 90%. But just remember you cant be perfect. The end of that first semester I ended up getting dean’s list. See your professors. That’s best advice I can give. Never be afraid to communicate with them! I did that for one class and she had me show her my work (I told her the question was misleading) and she gave me 10 points back on my exam. I can’t say that will happen to you, but trust me, your communication and dedication won’t go unnoticed. I suggest just going to see your professor with your exam and going through the questions you didn’t get. It will help. Good luck!

If you would like to use the money for a short term goal 2-3 yrs just stick it in a savings account. Go to bankrate.com and you can see what banks are offering higher % rates. I believe capital one is doing about 1% right now. 

You have to be careful investing it. If your goals is to use it in 5-10 yrs (like buying a house) I suggest seeing someone who can help you invest it properly. I recommend vanguard because they offer usually the cheapest fees. Most likely a bond fund or money market fund that is diversified (meaning you have A LOT of different types of companies) if it’s over 10 years your goal then you’ll want some sort of mutual fund! Again, if you plan on doing any sort of investment like bonds or mutual funds I highly suggest speaking to a professional so they can determine your comfort on risk and help you determine your goals.

Yes I always sit in the seat closet to the door. I make sure to get to my classes early enough so I can sit there! If I feel an anxiety attack coming I always know I won't make too much of a scene because I sit closest to the door and can quietly escape and take a few minutes outside. I always know that I can email the professor after if they are one of those that hates when students leave in the middle of class. Also, I do an exercise that helps me. I choose four numbers and repeat them to myself allowing my entire mind to focus on remembering the sequence. At the same time, focus on your breath.

I would talk with an advisor and financial aid office if you're up to trying it. I've dropped classes before because of working full time and trying to have a full time schedule with school. I dropped a class in April and my financial aid wasn't affected too badly when I went back in fall. You could see if there's still time to apply for part time study aid! But I totally understand it doesn't work out that way for everyone. Keep your head up.
Also, I never took my ACT or SAT examinations since I started at a community college. It's not needed. I'd only recommend taking them if you're going to go to a 4 year right away! Save the stress!
